problem: Classical graph planners (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) on topological maps built from exploration must handle noisy, probabilistic edge connectivity, and they ignore the rich visual features stored at nodes. Prior topological-memory navigation methods also need many random samples to populate the graph in a new environment.
motivation: Agents deployed in unseen indoor environments can explore first and build a topological map, but the map is uncertain because the connectivity estimates are noisy. Symbolic planners are only optimal with respect to the information they are given. Visual node features may carry cues, such as visible traversable space, that correct wrong connectivity estimates.
key_idea: Train a graph neural network to predict the next node on the ground-truth shortest path from a noisy probabilistic graph with visual node features. The GNN aggregates neighbor messages with a GRU, giving it an inductive bias that can represent the Bellman-Ford min update, and it is coupled with an RL point-goal local policy in a hierarchical image-goal navigator.
insight: A learned planner beats symbolic planners on the same uncertain graph because it can exploit patterns in the connection-probability matrix, even without visual features (H-SPL 0.468 vs 0.269 for the best symbolic baseline). Visual features add more (0.501). The GRU-based min-accumulation ablation (Fig. 7) shows the recurrent aggregation lets the model gain from more data, whereas the no-GRU variant does not. ModDrop-style mixing of ground-truth adjacency with probabilities gives about a 2.3% improvement (Fig. 5b).
method: Uncertain topological graph: nodes are visited places with CNN visual features and locations; edges carry distances D and learned line-of-sight probabilities E. It is built from an RL exploration rollout with an auxiliary link classifier f_link, and node count is capped by replacing the most redundant node under a Gaussian kernel.

Node embedding: each node has features [visual, edge probabilities, is-target flag, distances, one-hot id] plus a latent state r_i, and the target node is the one whose features are closest to the goal image by cosine distance.

Message passing: gated-linear messages m_ij = W1[n_i,n_j] ⊙ σ(W2[n_i,n_j]) are serialized over neighbors through a 2-layer GRU that mimics the sequential Bellman-Ford min update, followed by an MLP giving the new r_i, for k=6 steps.

Supervised training: each node predicts a softmax over the next node on the optimal path with cross-entropy against Dijkstra labels on ground-truth graphs. ModDrop-style masking of GT adjacency versus probabilities is tapered from 50% to 100% over 250 epochs, so the final model needs only probabilities.

Local policy: a recurrent AtariNet trained with PPO for point-goal navigation (dense geodesic reward, STOP action). It runs at most m=10 steps per waypoint, then the planner re-plans from the nearest node to the reached location.
Exploration policy: a PPO agent maximizing observed-area coverage, trained with an occupancy-grid reward, plus the auxiliary link loss.

setting.backbone: GNN planner with GRU aggregation (supervised) + recurrent AtariNet local policy (PPO) + PPO exploration policy with link classifier, all trained from scratch
setting.training_data: 72 Gibson training environments; 72,000 generated graphs (up to 74,000 in data-size study) with Dijkstra GT labels; local and exploration policies trained with 200M frames each
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (64x64) plus goal image; graph with visual node features
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: forward, turn left 10°, turn right 10° (plus STOP for the local policy); the high level picks graph nodes as waypoints
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration rollout to build the graph before each episode; local point-goal policy gets estimated locations from the planner. GT connectivity is used only in training.

numbers.extra: Evaluated on 16 held-out Gibson environments; explored graph built beforehand; 500 low-level step budget
Point-goals sampled from the action distribution instead of argmax; pre-explored graph

numbers.eval_set_note: paths of length ≥2 on uncertain graphs, 16 unseen environments
numbers.extra: Trained with 72,000 graphs; high-level planner only, graph space

numbers_note: Benchmarks are custom (a Gibson image-goal task with pre-explored graphs), not a canonical benchmark. Table 1a also has Neural (w/o visual) at Acc 0.251, H-SPL 0.468.
results: On uncertain graphs the neural planner reaches H-SPL 0.501 vs 0.269 for the best symbolic baseline (custom-cost Dijkstra). In the hierarchical image-goal task it achieves 0.983 SR / 0.877 SPL, vs 0.707 / 0.585 for the best symbolic planner and 0.548 / 0.248 for the recurrent image-goal RL agent. It comes close to the graph-oracle planner (0.963 / 0.882).
limitations: Requires a pre-exploration rollout to build the graph and assumes ground-truth graphs are available for supervised training; only evaluated in simulation (Habitat/Gibson) with no real robot.
Absolute accuracy of next-waypoint prediction on uncertain graphs is low (0.262), and the graph size is capped at 32 nodes; the goal is localized by simple cosine similarity of features.
The evaluation is on a custom task without comparison to established topological-memory navigation methods.
compares_to: Recurrent image-goal RL agent (siamese CNN + GRU, PPO)
